extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, judges, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and evaluating patent specifications: what a specification must disclose, how drawings and signatures function, what omissions or ambiguities will invalidate a patent, and how disclaimers/amendments operate. Focused on enablement, best mode, materials/proportions, and formal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / sufficiency of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be in such full, clear and exact terms, as to enable any one skilled in the art to which it appertains, to compound and use it without making any experiments of his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to machines and compositions; sufficiency is generally a question of fact for a jury. The test is whether a workman of ordinary skill can make and use the invention by following the directions, without needing to invent or add to them. Information required from other sources is excluded; reasonable data must be given. If experiments are necessary to produce beneficial effects, the patent is void. Examples/anti-patterns: a specification that only hints at the invention and throws the burden of experiment on the public is bad (Morgan v. Seaward).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose proportions/materials when essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Where materials and quantity are of the essence of the invention, the compositions and proportions must be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important for medicines, paints, and other compositions of matter. If the specification gives only names of substances without stating relative proportions, or states proportions ambiguously, the patent is void. Example in text: coal-dust to clay proportions for bricks; omission of essential proportions invalidates the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode / disclose most advantageous means known
rubrics_metrics.description: It is required as the price of the monopoly, that the patentee should enrol to the very best of his knowledge and judgment, the fullest and most sufficient description of the particulars on which the effect depended, the most advantageous mode known to the inventor, and any circumstance conducive to the advantageous operation, must be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must insert the best mode and known improved means for carrying out the invention at time of enrolment; failure to do so may be fatal. Must not mislead the public; the specification must give the best mode known and must not contain materially false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to describe matter within ordinary knowledge of workman
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not describe that which is within the ordinary knowledge of any workman who would be employed to put up the apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly known parts, processes, or terminology in the art may be omitted. Example: a condenser in constructing a gas apparatus need not be described. But if practical application involves particular knowledge, the specification must at least suggest that that thing is to be done (i.e., indicate the problem/step even if not fully instructing how to perform routine tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressed to persons skilled in the art (presumed technical knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is addressed to persons acquainted with the nature of the business; some technical knowledge is presumed on the part of those who will undertake to carry out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification using scientific terms that are understood by skilled persons is acceptable even if an ordinary person would not understand. Conversely, common language that misleads an ordinary person (when not professing scientific terms) renders the specification bad. The sufficiency standard is relative to ordinary skill in the relevant trade (neither highest engineers nor common laborers).

rubrics_metrics.name: No materially false statement in a material circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specification contains an untrue statement in a material circumstance, of such a nature that, if literally acted upon by a competent workman, it would mislead him and cause the experiment to fail, the specification is bad and the patent invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a jury finds that a competent workman could correct the error, a materially false statement that would mislead if followed literally invalidates the specification. Anti-pattern: asserting facts that are materially untrue without correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must teach the public / fully disclose the secret
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is intended to teach the public; it must fully disclose the secret, and contain nothing materially false or defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public is entitled to a fair, full, and true discovery as the price of the monopoly. Representations that are irrelevant, misleading, or included to puzzle will vitiate the specification. The specification must enable public practice after patent expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot rely on outside information or private instruction to make it work
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient that a skilful person should be able to find it out elsewhere; the invention must be effected by the directions contained in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information acquired from other sources (e.g., personal instruction of the inventor) is to be excluded in assessing sufficiency; the written specification (with drawings) must supply what is needed. Example: testimony that someone could make the device because they had verbal directions from the inventor is less weighty for public enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings constitute part of the specification and may supplement description
rubrics_metrics.description: When the nature of the case admits of drawings, the statute directs the patentee to accompany his specification with a drawing or drawings and written references; the object is both to distinguish the thing patented and to explain the mode of constructing it. Drawings annexed constitute part of the specification and may be used to explain or help out an otherwise imperfect description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification may be partly in writing and partly in drawing; if words and drawings together enable a skilful mechanic to perform the work and show the invention claimed, the specification is sufficient. Written references to drawings are not always necessary if the combination of drawing and text yields understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of drawings not always required but may be necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings need not be made to scale if a mechanic can make the subject from a perspective drawing; however, if the subject could not be made without many experiments unless the drawing is on a scale, then the specification (writing + drawing) is defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The drawing is open to explanation by the written description and vice versa; the ultimate test is public enablement without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal attestation/signature requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires a formal attestation of the specification and drawings: they must be signed by the inventor and by two witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It has been suggested that signing the specification referring to drawings attests the drawings, but whether both specification and drawings must be signed separately has not been definitively decided in the text. The statutory citation (Act of July 4, 1836) is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of something the patentee knows to be necessary is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission to mention in the specification anything which the patentee knows to be necessary for the beneficial enjoyment of his invention is a fatal defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor knows an element or step is necessary for the invention to work beneficially and omits it, the specification is invalid. By contrast, omission of something that only affects degree of benefit (but not sufficiency) may not be fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must state at least one method which will succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must state at least one method which will succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming a class of means without providing a successful method is insufficient. If a generic term covers many species but only one species actually works, the specification is bad as misleading the public. Example: claiming 'fossil salt' when only 'sal gem' will succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot claim an entire class if some members will not answer
rubrics_metrics.description: If a whole class of substances is stated as suitable and any one of them will not answer, the specification is bad as misleading the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All substances that will answer need not be enumerated, but the public must not be misled by a generic claim that includes non-working members. If a generally known substance contains foreign matter injurious to use, patentee must show a known easy method of removing it, or the specification is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of unnecessary or purposeless parts invalidates patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation and description of parts of no use, or without distinguishing to what purposes they are to be applied, will render the patent void; the specification must not puzzle the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inserting more parts than necessary (e.g., ten where four are sufficient) or including irrelevant features intended to confuse will vitiate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviation in precise dimensions that a skilled workman would correct is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: A deviation from the precise dimensions shown by the specification and model, so as to make different parts work together, is within the knowledge of any workman and is not fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical adjustments a workman of ordinary skill would make (e.g., slightly enlarging a part that is too small) do not invalidate the specification, so long as the specification enables construction with ordinary skill without new inventive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sufficient if apparatus works beneficially in simplest form
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that the apparatus described should produce the greatest amount of benefit; it is sufficient if persons acquainted with the trade would construct an apparatus productive of some benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great improvements made later do not render the original specification invalid provided the described apparatus can be used beneficially in its simplest form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments: adding new improvements after patent issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision exists for amendment of the specification by the addition of new improvements made after the patent has issued; the description of any such new improvement may be filed in the patent office and annexed to the original specification with a certificate of the time of annexure, and thereafter has the same effect as if embraced in the original specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory route (Act of 1836 §13) permits post-issue additions to be treated as part of the original specification when properly filed and certified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer for inadvertent overbroad claims and its procedural effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a patentee has, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, made his specification or claim too broad, claiming more than that of which he was the original inventor, he may make disclaimers of such parts of the thing patented as he does not claim to hold; disclaimers must be in writing, attested, recorded in the patent office on payment of a fee and become part of the original specification to the extent of the interest disclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different statutory provisions operate differently: one disclaimer (7th section of Act of 1837) applies to suits pending when filed; another (9th section) applies to suits brought after filing and preserves validity for bona fide parts the patentee truly owns. Filing timing and whether all parties (e.g., assignees) join affect legal consequences; failure to file timely disclaimers can bar costs or equitable relief. Example: Wyeth v. Stone discussion of procedural effects and limitations.
